name: Médoc
authorizedGrapesNote: Use the current INAO cahier des charges for official grape authorization and blend rules; this app separates those rules from common market shorthand.
officialRulesNote: Médoc AOC covers red wines from the northern Médoc district. Official production rules should be checked against INAO documents before publication-grade use.
commonPracticeNote: Often Merlot-leaning relative to the most famous gravel-croupe communes, though Cabernet Sauvignon remains important across many blends.
classificationContext: Less tied to the 1855 classified-growth narrative than Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux, and Saint-Estèphe, but important for understanding the northern Médoc as a whole.

terroir.learningPoint: The broader northern Médoc has a mix of gravel and heavier soils, so blends can vary from Cabernet-driven structure to rounder Merlot expression.

examNotes: Left Bank district appellation north of Haut-Médoc.
Useful contrast with Haut-Médoc: generally broader and often less classification-focused.

neighborComparisons.haut-medoc: Haut-Médoc is the southern district appellation and includes several famous commune appellations.
neighborComparisons.saint-estephe: Saint-Estèphe is a more tightly defined commune appellation with a stronger fine-wine identity.

name: Haut-Médoc
authorizedGrapesNote: Official grape varieties and production rules belong in the INAO source layer; common study language should not be treated as a legal rule.
officialRulesNote: Haut-Médoc AOC is a Left Bank district appellation for red Bordeaux. Some commune appellations sit within the broader Haut-Médoc geography.
commonPracticeNote: Commonly Cabernet Sauvignon-led on better gravel sites, with Merlot and other Bordeaux varieties contributing fruit, mid-palate, perfume, and structure.
classificationContext: Includes several classified-growth estates outside the most famous commune names, making it important in 1855 Classification study.

terroir.learningPoint: Gravel ridges favor Cabernet Sauvignon by improving drainage and heat retention, while heavier soils can support Merlot.

examNotes: Red wines only in classic Bordeaux blend style.
Know it as a broader category around and between the named commune appellations.

neighborComparisons.medoc: Haut-Médoc is generally the more classification-heavy southern district.
neighborComparisons.margaux: Margaux is a commune appellation often framed as more perfumed and elegant.
neighborComparisons.saint-julien: Saint-Julien is smaller and known for polished, balanced classified-growth wines.

name: Saint-Estèphe
authorizedGrapesNote: Separate official AOC authorization from the common statement that wines are usually Cabernet Sauvignon-dominant blends.
officialRulesNote: Saint-Estèphe AOC is a commune appellation for red Bordeaux. Exact authorized varieties and production constraints should be sourced from INAO.
commonPracticeNote: Often Cabernet Sauvignon-led, with Merlot important on cooler or clay-influenced soils.
classificationContext: Home to 1855 classified growths and often taught with emphasis on structure and longevity.

terroir.learningPoint: More clay influence than some neighboring communes can contribute firmness, power, and Merlot suitability.

examNotes: Northernmost of the four famous Médoc commune appellations in this study set.
Often described as firm, structured, and ageworthy.
Useful comparison point for Pauillac and Saint-Julien.

neighborComparisons.pauillac: Pauillac is often more associated with cassis, graphite, and first-growth prestige.
neighborComparisons.saint-julien: Saint-Julien is often described as more polished and harmonious.
neighborComparisons.medoc: Médoc AOC is broader and less commune-specific.

name: Pauillac
authorizedGrapesNote: Separate official AOC authorization from common real-world practice.
officialRulesNote: Pauillac AOC is a commune appellation for red Bordeaux. Use INAO documents for exact legal rules before publishing regulatory claims.
commonPracticeNote: Commonly Cabernet Sauvignon-dominant, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and other permitted Bordeaux varieties potentially involved depending on estate and vintage.
classificationContext: Central to the 1855 Classification, including three First Growths: Lafite Rothschild, Latour, and Mouton Rothschild.

terroir.learningPoint: Well-drained gravel helps Cabernet Sauvignon ripen and contributes to structure.

neighborComparisons.saint-estephe: Often firmer and more austere, with more clay influence.

name: Saint-Julien
authorizedGrapesNote: Treat grape authorization as an official-rule question and blend dominance as an observation about typical wines.
officialRulesNote: Saint-Julien AOC is a commune appellation for red Bordeaux. Legal production details should be sourced from INAO.
commonPracticeNote: Typically Cabernet Sauvignon-dominant, often praised for balance between power, finesse, fruit, and structure.
classificationContext: Small appellation with a high concentration of 1855 classified growths.

terroir.learningPoint: Consistent gravelly sites help explain Saint-Julien's reputation for complete, balanced Left Bank wines.

examNotes: Commune appellation between Pauillac and Margaux.
Often used as the textbook example of balance in the Médoc.
High classified-growth density despite its small size.

neighborComparisons.pauillac: Pauillac is often more powerful and graphite-driven.
neighborComparisons.margaux: Margaux is often more aromatic and silk-textured.
neighborComparisons.saint-estephe: Saint-Estèphe is often firmer and more robust.

name: Margaux
authorizedGrapesNote: Do not reduce Margaux to a single grape; it is a Bordeaux blend appellation with Cabernet Sauvignon commonly leading top wines.
officialRulesNote: Margaux AOC is a commune appellation for red Bordeaux. Exact legal rules should be tied to INAO source data.
commonPracticeNote: Often Cabernet Sauvignon-dominant in leading wines, with Merlot and other Bordeaux varieties shaping texture and aroma.
classificationContext: Home to Château Margaux, a First Growth, plus many other classified estates.

terroir.learningPoint: Margaux's best gravel sites support Cabernet Sauvignon while varied soils can add aromatic nuance and supple texture.

examNotes: Southernmost of the four famous Médoc commune appellations in this MVP.
Often described as perfumed, elegant, and refined.

neighborComparisons.saint-julien: Saint-Julien is often more compact and balanced.
neighborComparisons.pauillac: Pauillac is often more powerful, tannic, and graphite-led.
neighborComparisons.moulis-en-medoc: Moulis is inland and generally less classification-centered.

name: Moulis-en-Médoc
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for official authorization; common blends may lean Merlot or Cabernet Sauvignon depending on site and producer.
officialRulesNote: Moulis-en-Médoc AOC is an inland commune appellation for red Bordeaux.
commonPracticeNote: Often blends Merlot's roundness with Cabernet Sauvignon structure; style varies by gravel versus clay-limestone sites.
classificationContext: No 1855 classified growths, but the appellation has respected Cru Bourgeois and estate-level study relevance.

climate: less directly river-moderated than riverfront communes
terroir.learningPoint: Inland position and mixed soils make Moulis useful for studying how Médoc style shifts away from the most famous gravel croupes.

examNotes: One of the inland Médoc commune appellations.
Often less globally famous than Pauillac or Margaux but important for regional completeness.

neighborComparisons.listrac-medoc: Listrac is often presented as firmer and more rustic.
neighborComparisons.margaux: Margaux is generally more associated with perfume, finesse, and classified growths.
neighborComparisons.haut-medoc: Haut-Médoc is the broader surrounding district category.

name: Listrac-Médoc
authorizedGrapesNote: Official AOC authorization must be sourced separately from typical blend descriptions.
officialRulesNote: Listrac-Médoc AOC is an inland commune appellation for red Bordeaux.
commonPracticeNote: Often blends Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, with a reputation for firmer, more structured wines in some examples.
classificationContext: No 1855 classified growths; often studied through Cru Bourgeois and broader Médoc context.

terroir.learningPoint: Heavier and mixed soils can support Merlot and contribute to a firmer, less overtly polished profile than some riverfront communes.

examNotes: Useful reminder that not all Médoc commune appellations are 1855-classified-growth centers.

neighborComparisons.moulis-en-medoc: Moulis is often a little rounder depending on producer and site.
neighborComparisons.saint-julien: Saint-Julien is generally more polished and classification-focused.
neighborComparisons.haut-medoc: Haut-Médoc provides the wider district context.

name: Entre-deux-Mers
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for exact authorized varieties and proportions; study shorthand should not replace the cahier des charges.
officialRulesNote: Entre-deux-Mers AOC is principally associated with dry white Bordeaux from the area between the Garonne and Dordogne.
commonPracticeNote: Common examples are fresh, aromatic, Sauvignon Blanc-influenced dry whites, often blended with Sémillon and Muscadelle.
classificationContext: Not part of the 1855 Médoc classification story; it is important for understanding everyday dry white Bordeaux.

terroir.learningPoint: The between-rivers setting and mixed limestone/clay soils support crisp white Bordeaux styles as well as nearby sweet and red appellations.

examNotes: Located between the Garonne and Dordogne rivers.
Useful contrast with Médoc: white-led, not Cabernet/Merlot red-led.

neighborComparisons.premieres-cotes-de-bordeaux: Premières Côtes de Bordeaux sits nearer the Garonne-side slopes and has a different historical identity.
neighborComparisons.graves-de-vayres: Graves de Vayres is a smaller nearby appellation with both red and white context.

name: Entre-deux-Mers Haut-Benauge
authorizedGrapesNote: Confirm official grape and production rules with INAO before publication use.
officialRulesNote: Haut-Benauge is represented in the INAO source as a denomination within Entre-deux-Mers.
commonPracticeNote: Study it as a more specific Entre-deux-Mers dry white area rather than a separate fine-wine hierarchy like the Médoc communes.

terroir.learningPoint: The more specific denomination helps show that Bordeaux white-wine geography can be nested, just like red-wine areas.

examNotes: Specific denomination within the Entre-deux-Mers source data.
Useful for learning nested AOC geography.

neighborComparisons.entre-deux-mers: Entre-deux-Mers is the broader surrounding dry white appellation.

name: Cadillac
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for exact sweet-wine production rules and grape authorization.
officialRulesNote: Cadillac AOC is associated with sweet white Bordeaux from the Garonne-side slopes.
commonPracticeNote: Often botrytized or late-harvest influenced, with Sémillon providing texture and honeyed character.

terroir.learningPoint: Garonne-side humidity can support noble rot conditions, linking Cadillac conceptually to other sweet Bordeaux areas.

examNotes: Sweet white Bordeaux appellation in the Entre-Deux-Mers zone.
Different role from dry white Entre-deux-Mers.

neighborComparisons.loupiac: Loupiac is another small sweet white appellation on the Garonne-side slopes.
neighborComparisons.sainte-croix-du-mont: Sainte-Croix-du-Mont is also sweet white and geographically close.

name: Côtes de Bordeaux Cadillac
authorizedGrapesNote: Confirm official denomination rules with INAO; this app separates source denomination from general study shorthand.
officialRulesNote: The INAO source represents this as the Cadillac denomination within Côtes de Bordeaux.
commonPracticeNote: Typically Merlot-led red Bordeaux from slopes on the Garonne side of Entre-Deux-Mers.

terroir.learningPoint: The same broad area can support dry reds under Côtes de Bordeaux and sweet whites under Cadillac/Loupiac-style appellations.

examNotes: Useful contrast with sweet Cadillac AOC.
Part of the broader Bordeaux hillsides story.

neighborComparisons.cadillac: Cadillac itself is studied primarily as sweet white, while this denomination is dry red Côtes de Bordeaux context.

name: Loupiac
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for exact official sweet-wine rules.
officialRulesNote: Loupiac AOC is a small sweet white Bordeaux appellation near Cadillac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont.
commonPracticeNote: Often honeyed, botrytis-influenced, and Sémillon-led.

terroir.learningPoint: Loupiac helps explain why the Garonne-side slopes of Entre-Deux-Mers are important for sweet white Bordeaux.

neighborComparisons.cadillac: Cadillac is larger and nearby, also sweet white in this context.
neighborComparisons.sainte-croix-du-mont: Sainte-Croix-du-Mont is adjacent and similarly sweet-white focused.

name: Sainte-Croix-du-Mont
authorizedGrapesNote: Official rules should be tied to INAO before publication.
officialRulesNote: Sainte-Croix-du-Mont AOC is a small sweet white Bordeaux appellation on the Garonne side.
commonPracticeNote: Known for sweet white wines with honeyed, citrus, and botrytis-like notes depending on vintage and producer.

terroir.learningPoint: Its small footprint makes it a useful map example of highly specific sweet-wine geography inside greater Bordeaux.

examNotes: Often grouped in study with Cadillac and Loupiac.

neighborComparisons.loupiac: Loupiac is nearby and similarly sweet-white focused.
neighborComparisons.cadillac: Cadillac is another sweet white appellation in the same broader zone.

name: Premières Côtes de Bordeaux
authorizedGrapesNote: Use current INAO documents for official production scope and style rules.
officialRulesNote: Premières Côtes de Bordeaux is represented by the INAO source along the Garonne-side hillsides.
commonPracticeNote: Study as part of the Garonne-slope sweet white and hillside Bordeaux context.

terroir.learningPoint: The long Garonne-facing slope helps organize several Entre-Deux-Mers-side appellations on the map.

examNotes: Useful map anchor between Entre-deux-Mers and the small sweet white communes.
Check current INAO rules for publication-grade style claims.

neighborComparisons.cadillac: Cadillac is a smaller sweet white appellation within the same broad Garonne-side story.

name: Côtes de Bordeaux-Saint-Macaire
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for exact permitted styles and grape rules.
officialRulesNote: The INAO source includes Côtes de Bordeaux-Saint-Macaire as a distinct appellation.
commonPracticeNote: A smaller, less commonly encountered Bordeaux appellation useful for understanding the southern Entre-Deux-Mers/Garonne edge.

terroir.learningPoint: Saint-Macaire helps show that Bordeaux geography includes many small local AOCs beyond the globally famous names.

examNotes: Small Bordeaux appellation near the Garonne.
Less central than Entre-deux-Mers for most exams.
Good map context for local Bordeaux detail.

neighborComparisons.premieres-cotes-de-bordeaux: Both help define the Garonne-side edge of the Entre-Deux-Mers area.

name: Graves de Vayres
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for exact style and grape rules; this metadata is study shorthand.
officialRulesNote: Graves de Vayres is a small Bordeaux appellation represented in the INAO source near the Dordogne side.
commonPracticeNote: Can be studied as a local mixed-style appellation rather than a major global category.

terroir.learningPoint: The name points to gravelly local soils, but it is geographically separate from the larger Graves region south of Bordeaux.

examNotes: Do not confuse with the larger Graves region.
Useful Dordogne-side context for Entre-Deux-Mers expansion.

neighborComparisons.entre-deux-mers: Entre-deux-Mers is broader and primarily dry white in classic study shorthand.

name: Saint-Émilion
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for official authorization; study shorthand is Merlot with important Cabernet Franc.
officialRulesNote: Saint-Émilion is a Right Bank red-wine AOC; Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is a related stricter designation not separately displayed in this MVP.
commonPracticeNote: Commonly Merlot-led, with Cabernet Franc contributing perfume, freshness, and structure.
classificationContext: Know the separate Saint-Émilion classification context, especially for advanced Bordeaux study.

terroir.learningPoint: Limestone and clay-limestone sites help explain Merlot richness with Cabernet Franc freshness and ageworthy structure.

examNotes: Merlot and Cabernet Franc are the key study grapes.
Contrast with Pomerol as often more limestone-driven and classification-focused.

neighborComparisons.pomerol: Pomerol is generally smaller, often plusher, and has no formal classification.
neighborComparisons.montagne-saint-emilion: Montagne-Saint-Émilion is a satellite appellation north of Saint-Émilion.

name: Pomerol
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for official rules; common exam shorthand emphasizes Merlot dominance.
officialRulesNote: Pomerol is a small Right Bank red-wine appellation.
commonPracticeNote: Often Merlot-dominant, producing plush, concentrated reds with refined tannins.
classificationContext: No formal classification, despite global prestige and famous estates.

terroir.learningPoint: Clay-rich soils are central to why Merlot can produce deep, plush, ageworthy wines here.

examNotes: Merlot is the main blind-tasting clue.

neighborComparisons.saint-emilion: Saint-Émilion is larger and more varied, often with more visible Cabernet Franc character.
neighborComparisons.lalande-de-pomerol: Lalande-de-Pomerol is nearby and often a more accessible Right Bank comparison.

name: Lalande-de-Pomerol
authorizedGrapesNote: Check INAO for official grape rules; study language follows Right Bank Merlot-led blends.
officialRulesNote: Lalande-de-Pomerol is a Right Bank red-wine AOC north of Pomerol.
commonPracticeNote: Usually Merlot-led and approachable relative to the most famous Pomerol wines.

terroir.learningPoint: The mix of gravel and clay supports Merlot-led blends with Right Bank softness and freshness.

neighborComparisons.pomerol: Pomerol is generally denser, more prestigious, and more expensive.

name: Fronsac

officialRulesNote: Fronsac is a Right Bank red-wine AOC west of Saint-Émilion and Pomerol.
commonPracticeNote: Can show structured, earthy Merlot-led reds with good value.

terroir.learningPoint: Limestone and clay can give Fronsac more firmness and earthy structure than simple Right Bank shorthand suggests.

examNotes: Right Bank appellation west of Pomerol.
Canon Fronsac is the smaller related appellation.

neighborComparisons.canon-fronsac: Canon Fronsac is smaller and often treated as a more specific Fronsac-area appellation.

name: Canon Fronsac
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for official rules; study shorthand is Merlot-led Right Bank red.
officialRulesNote: Canon Fronsac is a small Right Bank red-wine AOC near Fronsac.
commonPracticeNote: Often structured, savory, and limestone-influenced.

terroir.learningPoint: The smaller limestone-influenced area can give wines freshness, firmness, and savory depth.

neighborComparisons.fronsac: Fronsac is the broader neighboring reference point.

officialRulesNote: A Saint-Émilion satellite appellation for dry red wines.
commonPracticeNote: Usually Merlot-led, often slightly less concentrated than top Saint-Émilion but similar in style.

terroir.learningPoint: Satellite appellations help map the wider limestone and clay-limestone Right Bank landscape.

examNotes: Useful for Right Bank hierarchy study.

neighborComparisons.saint-emilion: Saint-Émilion is the major reference appellation.

name: Lussac-Saint-Émilion
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for official rules; common practice is Merlot-led Right Bank blend.
officialRulesNote: A Saint-Émilion satellite appellation for red wines.
commonPracticeNote: Often approachable Merlot-led reds with red and black plum fruit.

terroir.learningPoint: Clay-limestone supports Merlot ripeness while preserving structure and freshness.

examNotes: Part of the Right Bank study cluster.

neighborComparisons.montagne-saint-emilion: Both are Saint-Émilion satellites with Merlot-led profiles.

name: Puisseguin-Saint-Émilion
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for official rules; common study framing is Merlot-led Right Bank blend.
officialRulesNote: A Saint-Émilion satellite appellation for red wines.
commonPracticeNote: Typically Merlot-led, with savory red-fruit and plum notes.

terroir.learningPoint: Limestone and clay help place it in the same broad study family as Saint-Émilion.

examNotes: Good satellite appellation for map hierarchy.

name: Saint-Georges-Saint-Émilion
authorizedGrapesNote: Use INAO for official rules; common study framing is Merlot-led Right Bank blend.
officialRulesNote: A small Saint-Émilion satellite appellation for red wines.
commonPracticeNote: Usually Merlot-led with moderate structure and Right Bank savory fruit.

terroir.learningPoint: A small satellite that reinforces the limestone/clay-limestone Right Bank pattern.

neighborComparisons.montagne-saint-emilion: Montagne-Saint-Émilion is the larger nearby satellite reference.

name: Graves

neighborComparisons.pessac-leognan: Pessac-Léognan is the more prestigious northern Graves appellation.
neighborComparisons.graves-de-vayres: Graves de Vayres is a separate small Dordogne-side appellation.
